content: The term micronutrient powder (MNP) refers to a supplement containing multiple essential micronutrients. Super Cereal Plus (SCP) is a fortified cereal product, and small-quantity lipid-based nutrient supplement (SQ-LNS) is a nutrient-dense supplement designed to provide essential lipids and micronutrients in small amounts. The original scenario was designed to reflect real-world dietary patterns, using survey data to estimate the percentage of energy derived from various food subgroups, excluding breast milk. The energy contribution from breast milk was fixed for each age group, consistent with modeled scenarios. The total dietary energy was calculated based on the estimated energy requirement (EER) for a small infant or child in each age group. Specifically, the EER was determined for a girl at the lower end of the age range and the 25th percentile for weight-for-age. Nutrients were included in the analysis if their dietary content fell below 98% of the nutrient reference value (NRV) in any scenario. Nutrients that reached only 9% of the NRV were highlighted in gold. For infants and children, the EER was calculated differently depending on the scenario. For the original scenario, the EER for an average-sized child was determined by averaging the EER for boys and girls at the midpoint of the age range and the 50th percentile for weight-for-age. The study explored whether target nutrient needs could be met using unfortified best-case food patterns. Weekly feasible best-case food patterns were modeled to determine if unfortified foods and beverages could meet nutrient needs, given a fixed percentage of energy from breast milk for each age. When feasible patterns failed to meet all nutrient needs, liberalized best-case patterns were modeled to address gaps. Except for iron during infancy, feasible best-case patterns met all target nutrient needs at middle and high energy levels. However, for infants aged 9 months, additional gaps were identified for calcium, potassium, and zinc. Across all energy levels and age groups in infancy, the iron content of the modeled food patterns ranged from 24% to 45% of the NRV, increasing with higher energy levels. Liberalized best-case patterns, modeled only for infants, allowed up to seven daily servings per week for all food subgroups. These patterns reduced but did not eliminate iron gaps during infancy. The iron content in liberalized patterns ranged from 41% to 71% of the NRV. Macronutrient profiles were reasonable, with protein providing 13–16% of energy, fat 40–45%, and carbohydrates 43–49%. However, all patterns were low in vitamin D, which was not a target nutrient in the analysis. Vitamin D levels ranged from 3–24% of the NRV in feasible patterns and 7–11% in liberalized patterns. The NRV assumes minimal sunlight exposure, and the analysis did not optimize vitamin D content. The study also examined nutrient quantities against upper intake levels (ULs). For example, copper ULs were based on liver damage in individuals with copper homeostasis defects, and zinc ULs were exceeded in some scenarios, particularly with daily SQ-LNS supplementation. The authors noted uncertainty about the clinical significance of these values. Feasible best-case food patterns were diverse, with diversity increasing with age and energy level, ranging from 10 to 20 food subgroups per week. Liberalized patterns included fewer subgroups but remained diverse. Patterns included 5–7 of the 8 food groups in the WHO/UNICEF IYCF diversity indicator. Patterns for younger infants included minimal staple foods, providing 4–5% of energy, with only whole-grain breakfast cereals selected. For older infants, staple foods contributed 9–13% of energy. For non-breastfed children at middle and high energy levels, staple foods contributed 37–38% of energy, reflecting a minimization of protein in these scenarios. Selected staple foods were primarily whole grains, while refined grains were more typical in many settings. All feasible patterns included animal-source protein foods and diverse vegetable subgroups. Most patterns also included plant-source protein foods. Except for the youngest infants, all patterns included fruit. Small amounts of dairy were included in some patterns for breastfed infants, while larger amounts were included for non-breastfed infants. Maximum weekly quantities of vegetables were selected in all feasible patterns, including dark green leafy vegetables. Immature peas/beans and liver were selected at maximum allowed amounts in most scenarios. The study highlighted significant differences between best-case and typical IYCF food patterns, particularly in the quantity and diversity of vegetables and protein food subgroups. Parameters were based on high-end observed distributions within datasets, with quantities based on medians observed in high-consumption countries and diversity parameters reflecting the 90th percentile in countries with high diversity. Sensitivity analyses modeled scenarios with lower iron absorption (5%) and no flesh foods allowed. In these scenarios, significant iron gaps were observed for both breastfed (47% of NRV) and non-breastfed children (65% of NRV). No other target nutrient gaps were identified, though gaps for carbohydrates and vitamin D remained. Food patterns differed between higher and lower absorption scenarios, with higher protein and lower carbohydrate energy percentages in lower absorption scenarios. The largest differences were in fruit (lower amounts with lower absorption) and protein foods (higher amounts of eggs and plant-source protein foods with lower absorption and no flesh foods allowed). Modifications to food patterns had major impacts on nutrient gaps for the youngest age group, where only ~150 kilocalories were available for complementary foods and beverages. Fewer impacts were observed for older IYCF groups. Certain modified patterns exceeded AMDRs or ULs for copper and zinc. The study noted that further modeling could potentially address these excesses but emphasized that the objective was to answer research questions rather than develop specific food-based recommendations. For 9-month-old infants, many modifications resulted in additional nutrient gaps, particularly for minerals and occasionally B vitamins. Iron gaps increased or new gaps were introduced when food groups or subgroups were eliminated, staple foods were restricted to one type, staple food quantities were increased, or unhealthy items were introduced. Patterns with monotonous staple foods remained low in iron and introduced new gaps. Patterns including unhealthy items had new gaps for minerals and B vitamins, even when included only one day per week. Gaps increased with more frequent inclusion of unhealthy items. In summary, meeting nutrient needs from an unfortified food supply for breastfed infants in this age group requires diverse diets with daily animal-source protein foods, ample and diverse vegetables, very limited staple foods, and no refined grains or unhealthy items. Even in the liberalized best-case scenario, iron needs could not be met. Fortified products designed for IYCF had varying effects on nutrient gaps, depending on the product and energy level. MNPs eliminated the iron gap but introduced a magnesium gap.
